325	### Manual filtering: file types
326	
327	Over time, you might notice that you use the same glob patterns over and over.
328	For example, you might find yourself doing a lot of searches where you only
329	want to see results for Rust files:
330	
331	```
332	$ rg 'fn run' -g '*.rs'
333	```
334	
335	Instead of writing out the glob every time, you can use ripgrep's support for
336	file types:
337	
338	```
339	$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
340	```
341	
342	or, more succinctly,
343	
344	```
345	$ rg 'fn run' -trust
346	```
347	
348	The way the `--type` flag functions is simple. It acts as a name that is
349	assigned to one or more globs that match the relevant files. This lets you
350	write a single type that might encompass a broad range of file extensions. For
351	example, if you wanted to search C files, you'd have to check both C source
352	files and C header files:
353	
354	```
355	$ rg 'int main' -g '*.{c,h}'
356	```
357	
358	or you could just use the C file type:
359	
360	```
361	$ rg 'int main' -tc
362	```
363	
364	Just as you can write blacklist globs, you can blacklist file types too:
365	
366	```
367	$ rg clap --type-not rust
368	```
369	
370	or, more succinctly,
371	
372	```
373	$ rg clap -Trust
374	```
375	
376	That is, `-t` means "include files of this type" where as `-T` means "exclude
377	files of this type."
378	
379	To see the globs that make up a type, run `rg --type-list`:
380	
381	```
382	$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
383	make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
384	```
385	
386	By default, ripgrep comes with a bunch of pre-defined types. Generally, these
387	types correspond to well known public formats. But you can define your own
388	types as well. For example, perhaps you frequently search "web" files, which
389	consist of JavaScript, HTML and CSS:
390	
391	```
392	$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
393	```
394	
395	or, more succinctly,
396	
397	```
398	$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
399	```
400	
401	The above command defines a new type, `web`, corresponding to the glob
402	`*.{html,css,js}`. It then applies the new filter with `-tweb` and searches for
403	the pattern `title`. If you ran
404	
405	```
406	$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' --type-list
407	```
408	
409	Then you would see your `web` type show up in the list, even though it is not
410	part of ripgrep's built-in types.
411	
412	It is important to stress here that the `--type-add` flag only applies to the
413	current command. It does not add a new file type and save it somewhere in a
414	persistent form. If you want a type to be available in every ripgrep command,
415	then you should either create a shell alias:
416	
417	```
418	alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
419	```
420	
421	or add `--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}` to your ripgrep configuration file.
422	([Configuration files](#configuration-file) are covered in more detail later.)
423	
424	#### The special `all` file type
425	
426	A special option supported by the `--type` flag is `all`. `--type all` looks
427	for a match in any of the supported file types listed by `--type-list`,
428	including those added on the command line using `--type-add`. It's equivalent
429	to the command `rg --type agda --type asciidoc --type asm ...`, where `...`
430	stands for a list of `--type` flags for the rest of the types in `--type-list`.
431	
432	As an example, let's suppose you have a shell script in your current directory,
433	`my-shell-script`, which includes a shell library, `my-shell-library.bash`.
434	Both `rg --type sh` and `rg --type all` would only search for matches in
435	`my-shell-library.bash`, not `my-shell-script`, because the globs matched
436	by the `sh` file type don't include files without an extension. On the
437	other hand, `rg --type-not all` would search `my-shell-script` but not
438	`my-shell-library.bash`.
439	
440	### Replacements
441	
442	ripgrep provides a limited ability to modify its output by replacing matched
443	text with some other text. This is easiest to explain with an example. Remember
444	when we searched for the word `fast` in ripgrep's README?

{"file_path":"<path>","content":"# Filtering by file type in ripgrep

If you search text for a living, you already know the routine: you only want the
Rust files, or everything *except* the minified JavaScript, or just this one
odd extension your team invented. You can spell that out with globs every time
(`rg 'fn run' -g '*.rs'`), but ripgrep gives you a shorter, named way to say the
same thing. A *type* is just a name assigned to one or more globs. Four flags
manage them: `-t/--type`, `-T/--type-not`, `--type-add`, and `--type-list`.

## `-t/--type`: search only this type

`--type` limits the search to files matching a named type.

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
$ rg 'fn run' -trust
```

The two lines are equivalent; the short form takes its value with no space.
Because `rust` bundles the relevant globs, you don't have to remember whether
you want `*.rs` alone or something broader. The C type covers both source and
headers, so `rg 'int main' -tc` searches `*.c` and `*.h` at once.

You can repeat the flag. `rg -trust -tpython` searches both Rust and Python
files. Note that `--type` has lower precedence than the `-g/--glob` flag and
than any rules found in ignore files, so a `.gitignore` entry or an explicit
glob still wins.

## `-T/--type-not`: search everything but this type

`--type-not` is the mirror image. Where `-t` means "include files of this
type", `-T` means "exclude files of this type."

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

You can repeat it, and you can mix the two on one command line. `rg -Trust
-ttoml -Tjson` reads left to right, so each flag adds to the running set of
inclusions and exclusions.

## The special `all` type

Both `--type` and `--type-not` accept the special value `all`.

`--type all` behaves as if you had passed `--type` for every type ripgrep
knows, including any you added on the command line. The effect is a "whitelist"
search: ripgrep only searches files it *recognizes* through its type
definitions, and skips anything with an unknown extension.

`--type-not all` is the inverse "blacklist" search: ripgrep only searches files
that are *unrecognized*. This is worth a moment of thought, because recognition
hinges on the globs, not on what the file really is. Suppose you have a shell
script named `my-shell-script` (no extension) that sources
`my-shell-library.bash`. Both `rg --type sh` and `rg --type all` search only
`my-shell-library.bash`, because the `sh` globs don't match an extensionless
name. Conversely, `rg --type-not all` searches `my-shell-script` but not
`my-shell-library.bash`.

## `--type-add`: define your own type

ripgrep ships with a large set of predefined types for well-known public
formats. When those don't cover your work, define your own. Say you often
search "web" files — JavaScript, HTML, and CSS:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
```

The syntax is `name:glob`. Only one glob per flag, so repeat `--type-add` to
add more — or fold them into a single brace glob:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

That defines `web` as `*.{html,css,js}`, then searches for `title` in matching
files. Unless you also pass `--type-clear`, added globs join any globs already
defined for that name rather than replacing them. Type names must consist only
of Unicode letters or numbers; punctuation isn't allowed.

You can also build a type out of existing types with the `include` directive.
It takes one or more already-defined type names, comma-separated, and imports
their globs:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md'
```

That makes `src` match C++, Python, and Markdown files. You can keep adding
plain globs to it afterward:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo'
```

One caveat worth stressing: `--type-add` applies only to the current command.
It is not saved anywhere. To make a type available every time, either alias
ripgrep —

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

— or put `--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}` in your configuration file.

## `--type-list`: see what's defined

To review the types, run `--type-list`. Each type prints on its own line,
followed by a `:` and a comma-delimited list of its globs:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

The listing accounts for any `--type-add` and `--type-clear` flags on the same
command, so a type you define appears in the output even though it isn't one of
ripgrep's built-ins. That makes `--type-list` the quickest way to confirm a
custom definition matches what you meant before you rely on it.

for a match in any of the supported file types listed by `--type-list`,

### Default type list

### Matcher module & semantics
`<path> The module-level doc (lines 1–85) contains runnable doctests demonstrating select, negate, custom `add`/`add_def`, and the `include` form (`builder.add_def("bar:include:foo,cpp")`, lines 72–84).

How the pieces work (from source):

- **How `--type-add` syntax is parsed** — `add_def` (lines 442–479). Splits the spec on `:`:
  - **2 parts** `{name}:{glob}` (lines 445–452): root definition — associates `name` with a single `glob`. Empty name or glob → `Error::InvalidDefinition`.
  - **3 parts** `{name}:include:{comma-list}` (lines 453–476): the middle part *must* literally be `include` (line 457), else error. The comma-separated type names must all already be defined — checked up-front and fails fast (`Error::InvalidDefinition`) if any is missing (lines 462–467). Each referenced type's globs are copied into the new type (lines 468–474). Because included types must already exist, ordering matters and self/forward references fail (see tests around line 573–580, `combo:include:html,qwerty` fails and leaves state unchanged).
  - Any other number of `:`-parts → `Error::InvalidDefinition` (line 477). Note: since it splits on all `:`, a 3-part spec is only ever an include; a glob containing a `:` is not supported in that position.
- **"Only one glob can be added at a time"**: `add` (lines 417–431) pushes exactly one glob onto the named type's glob vector, creating the type entry if absent. Type names must be non-`all` and all-alphanumeric (`is_alphanumeric`), else `Error::InvalidDefinition` (line 418) — this is the "Unicode letters or numbers only" rule from the help text.
- **`--type-clear`** maps to `TypesBuilder::clear` (lines 407–410): `self.types.remove(name)` — removes the whole definition; globs can be re-added afterward.
- **`-t` / `--type` = `select`** (lines 381–390); **`-T` / `--type-not` = `negate`** (lines 395–404). The special value `all` is expanded here: `select("all")`/`negate("all")` push a Select/Negate selection for **every** currently-defined type name (lines 382–385 / 396–399). This is why `all` reflects `--type-add`-defined custom types too.
- **How globs are matched** — `build` (lines 322–362): every glob of every selected type is compiled with `GlobBuilder::new(glob).literal_separator(true)` (lines 339–340), i.e. `*` does **not** cross `/`, and added to a single `GlobSet`. `matched` (lines 261–300) matches against the **file name only** (`file_name(path)`, line 273), not the full path. Directories never match (line 268). Multiple globs may match; **the highest-precedence match is the last one** in the set (lines 284–288), and whether that final matching glob belongs to a negated selection decides Ignore vs Whitelist (lines 289–293).
- **How negation composes / precedence** (documented at lines 255–260 and implemented in `matched`):
  - A path matching a **selected** type → `Whitelist`.
  - A path matching a **negated** type → `Ignore`.
  - If at least one type is **selected** (`has_selected`, line 324) and the path matches **nothing** → `Ignore` (lines 295–296). This is the "whitelist mode" behavior: selecting any type excludes everything not selected.
  - If there are only negations (no selection) and the path matches nothing → `Match::None` (pass-through, lines 297–298).
  - When both select and negate globs match a path, the **last-added** matching glob wins (order-dependent precedence), so mixing `-t` and `-T` on overlapping types resolves by set order, not by a fixed select-over-negate rule.
  - Per the `-t`/`--type` help (defs.rs lines 6795–6796), the whole type filter has **lower precedence than `--glob` and ignore-file rules**.

The `select`/`negate`/`clear`/`add` operations are all recorded as ordered `TypeChange` entries in `LowArgs.type_changes` at parse time (defs.rs `update` methods, e.g. lines 6805–6809, 6895–6898, 6955–6959, 7027–7031), so `-t`, `-T`, `--type-add`, and `--type-clear` may each be repeated and are applied in command-line order (see tests at defs.rs lines 6830–6831 and 7059–7063, e.g. `-Trust -ttoml -Tjson` yields `[negate(rust), select(toml), negate(json)]`).
